text: End of course test, track one. Good afternoon. It's great to see you all here today. I'm Sandy Dickinson and I'm going to focus on three important construction innovations. Before we begin, however, I'd just like to mention that my company, Innovators Construct, will be at next week's Architectural Design Conference in London, where I'll be launching our energy-saving underfloor heating product. Please do come along to the event if you can. Right, so let's get started. First, I'd like to talk to you about a concept called Digital Twins. A digital twin is basically a computer-made copy of an asset, which can be an object, a system or a process. It uses a computer program that takes real-world data about the asset and predicts how that data will affect the asset. This means that the digital twin can show us how the asset will perform without the need to test it in the real world. How can the digital twin help construction projects? Well, it can include all the information from design through to construction and then operation. Because the digital twin can analyze data as it arrives, it helps project managers to make early decisions and avoid unexpected costs. Or, if additional costs are necessary, it allows project managers to remain in control throughout the cycle of the project. The digital twin was implemented for the Thames Estuary Flood Management Project, where it analyzed 70 years of historical data. By getting data up to 25 years faster than other more historical methods, it transformed the way developers and architects work together. Next, I want to talk to you about augmented reality. Augmented reality technology has come a long way since it was invented in 1968 by Ivan Sutherland. He was a computer graphics engineer as well as a teacher, and he developed the first augmented reality display system with the help of his students. Augmented reality technologies, like smart glasses, give you an interactive experience that mixes the real world with a computer-made one. For example, this means you can look at a house that is being built right now, but the glasses can show you what it will look like when it is finished. It is a three-dimensional, or 3D, example of reality, and is quite amazing. Using AR technology, we can put the potential customers directly inside a building at the design stage. Furthermore, when working on site, engineers wearing smart glasses see where there are electrical wires hidden behind walls. The AR technology, in this example, would act as a safety or alarm system. Finally, I want to talk about robots. For many of us, robots are a thing of films. Most of us have seen R2-D2 or C-3PO in George Lucas' Star Wars. These lovable robots with different personalities and behaviors were, and still are, popular with cinema fans today. Robots are already in use today within the construction industry in a range of shapes and sizes. They can lay bricks, move materials, and 3D print, among other things. However, the way of the future is swarm robotics, a new experimental technology that is developing very fast. What is swarm robotics? Simply put, swarm robotics is a multi-robot system which consists of a large number of simple, individual robots. Think of it like a family of bees, called a swarm, that work individually but for the benefit of the whole family. One of the advantages of swarm robotics is that it can be designed to work on large-scale projects, and they are a self-organizing network, making them extremely efficient. Several companies have started working on the next stage of robots and robot networks, which is the development of mobility, the ability to move from one place to another. This is positive news for architecture, design, and construction industries, as the ability to use robots on rough ground, which is hilly or rocky, for example, would be a huge step forward from where we are now. Right, well, that's all we have time for today. I think you'll agree from these innovations that this is by far the most exciting time to be involved in the construction industry as a developer, engineer, or architect. Thank you. Now, any questions?
